story: A national emergency order on foreign bulk-power system equipment borrows the Federal Power Act's own definition of the bulk-power system, adds a 69,000 volt line, and drops the statute's Alaska sentence, while Alaska's own reliability council calls the Railbelt islanded and a DOE comment window closes October 9th

claims.claim: Executive Order 14421 is dated August 26th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: Executive Order 14421 of August 26, 2026
claims.notes: Dateline as printed in the Presidential Documents section. Confirmed on two separate fetches.

claims.claim: The title of Executive Order 14421 is Declaring a National Emergency To Secure the United States Bulk-Power System.
claims.value: Declaring a National Emergency To Secure the United States Bulk-Power System
claims.verbatim: Declaring a National Emergency To Secure the United States Bulk-Power System
claims.notes: Capital T in To is as printed.

claims.claim: Executive Order 14421 was published in the Federal Register on August 31st, 2026 beginning at page 55995 of volume 91.
claims.notes: Pages 55995 to 55999, volume 91 issue 167.

claims.claim: The order's stated rationale names data centers and artificial intelligence as drivers of the Nation's dependence on reliable electricity.
claims.verbatim: The rapid growth of advanced manufacturing, data centers, artificial intelligence, and defense production has increased the Nation's dependence on abundant, reliable electricity and magnified the consequences of a successful attack or supply disruption on the bulk-power system.
claims.notes: Transcribed in four consecutive fragments and reassembled.

claims.claim: Section 5(a) of the order defines the bulk-power system around facilities necessary for operating an interconnected electric energy transmission network.
claims.verbatim: facilities and control systems necessary for operating an interconnected electric energy transmission network
claims.notes: Clause (i). Clause (ii) reads electric energy from generation facilities needed to maintain electric system reliability.

claims.claim: The order's own definition covers transmission lines rated at 69,000 volts or more and excludes local distribution facilities.
claims.verbatim: For the purpose of this order, this definition includes transmission lines rated at 69,000 volts (69 kV) or more, but does not include facilities used in the local distribution of electric energy.
claims.notes: Reassembled from three consecutive fragments. This is the threshold the Alaska angle turns on.

claims.claim: Section 5(b) lists substation transformers, grid-connected inverters, battery energy storage systems and uninterruptible power supply systems among covered bulk-power system electric equipment.
claims.value: substation transformers, grid-connected inverters, battery energy storage systems
claims.verbatim: substation transformers; utility-scale and other grid-connected inverters; battery energy storage systems; and uninterruptible power supply systems supporting critical infrastructure
claims.notes: The full list also names reactors, capacitors, current coupling capacitors, large generators, small generators, backup generators, substation voltage regulators, shunt capacitor equipment, automatic circuit reclosers, instrument transformers, coupling capacity voltage transformers, protective relaying, metering equipment, high voltage circuit breakers, generation turbines, industrial control systems including remote terminal units and programmable logic controllers and intelligent electronic devices, distributed control systems, and safety instrumented systems.

claims.claim: The order is issued under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and the National Emergencies Act.
claims.verbatim: including the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.) (IEEPA), the National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1601 et seq.) (NEA)

claims.claim: The order declares a national emergency with respect to the foreign supply of bulk-power system electric equipment.
claims.verbatim: find that the situation with respect to the foreign supply of bulk-power system electric equipment constitutes an unusual and extraordinary threat

claims.claim: The order gives the Secretary of Energy 120 days to publish rules or regulations implementing its authorities.
claims.verbatim: Within 120 days of the date of this order, the Secretary
claims.notes: 120 days from August 26th, 2026 lands in late December 2026.

claims.claim: The order gives the Secretary of Energy 180 days to submit recommended revisions to the Federal Acquisition Regulation.
claims.verbatim: shall develop and submit a set of recommended revisions to the Federal Acquisition Regulation
claims.notes: The FAR Council then has 90 days after the recommendations to consider proposed amendments.

claims.claim: No geographic exclusion appears in the text of Executive Order 14421 as published, and the words Alaska, Hawaii, islanded and non-contiguous appear nowhere in it.
claims.verbatim: For the purpose of this order, this definition includes transmission lines rated at 69,000 volts (69 kV) or more, but does not include facilities used in the local distribution of electric energy.
claims.notes: ABSENCE CLAIM. Verified by two independent full-document reads. The verbatim field holds the operative scope sentence, which is where a geographic carve out would sit, since an absence cannot be quoted. The related word interconnected DOES appear in Section 5(a)(i), so this claim must never be extended to interconnection language.

claims.claim: The Department of Energy Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response published a request for information titled Securing the United States Bulk-Power System.
claims.value: Securing the United States Bulk-Power System
claims.verbatim: ACTION: Request for information (RFI).

claims.claim: The DOE request for information was published on September 9th, 2026 starting at page 57322 of Federal Register volume 91.
claims.notes: Volume 91, issue 173, pages 57322 to 57328.

claims.claim: The DOE request for information carries the Regulation Identifier Number 1901-AB79.
claims.verbatim: RIN 1901-AB79
claims.notes: Use this rather than the docket string. The document prints the docket two different ways, so the RIN is the unambiguous identifier.

claims.claim: Comments on the DOE request for information are accepted on or before October 9th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: Written responses, data, and information are requested and will be accepted on or before October 9, 2026.
claims.notes: Thirty days from publication.

claims.claim: Question A-2 of the request for information asks commenters to identify equipment-specific voltage, capacity, connectivity, function, location or criticality thresholds.
claims.verbatim: Identify any equipment-specific voltage, capacity, connectivity, function, location, or criticality thresholds that would improve clarity without creating material security gaps.
claims.notes: Confirmed verbatim on two independent fetches. The word location in that list is the closest the RFI comes to inviting a geographic argument.

claims.claim: DOE states the request for information is meant to inform its actions to implement the executive order.
claims.value: to inform DOE actions to implement the Executive order
claims.verbatim: the Department of Energy (DOE or the Department) is seeking information from industry and other stakeholders to inform DOE actions to implement the Executive order.
claims.notes: The RFI informs implementation. The 120 day rulemaking is what sets scope. Never say the RFI sets the scope.

claims.claim: The DOE request for information as published raises no geographic or islanded system question, and the words Alaska, Hawaii, islanded and non-contiguous appear nowhere in it.
claims.verbatim: Identify any equipment-specific voltage, capacity, connectivity, function, location, or criticality thresholds that would improve clarity without creating material security gaps.
claims.notes: ABSENCE CLAIM. Verified by two independent full-document reads. The verbatim field holds the scoping question where such a carve out would naturally be raised.

claims.claim: Section 215 of the Federal Power Act states that its provisions do not apply to Alaska or Hawaii.
claims.verbatim: The provisions of this section do not apply to Alaska or Hawaii.
claims.source_outlet: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, United States Code
claims.notes: Subsection (k), headed Alaska and Hawaii. Independently confirmed word for word at Cornell LII. This is the hinge of the story, so it was verified against two hosts.

claims.claim: 16 U.S.C. 824o is the Federal Power Act electric reliability section that created the national electric reliability organization regime.
claims.value: Section 215 of the Federal Power Act
claims.verbatim: 16 U.S. Code 824o - Electric reliability
claims.notes: Secondary reproduction of the statute. Pair with C20, whose primary is uscode.house.gov.

claims.claim: The Federal Power Act reliability section defines the bulk-power system in nearly the same words the executive order uses.
claims.verbatim: facilities and control systems necessary for operating an interconnected electric energy transmission network (or any portion thereof); and electric energy from generation facilities needed to maintain transmission system reliability.
claims.notes: Subsection (a)(1). The statute says transmission system reliability where the order says electric system reliability, and the statute carries no 69 kV sentence.

claims.claim: The Railbelt Reliability Council describes itself as Alaska's first electric reliability organization.
claims.verbatim: Alaska's First Electric Reliability Organization

claims.claim: The Railbelt Reliability Council calls the Railbelt grid islanded.
claims.verbatim: islanded Railbelt grid's unique challenges
claims.notes: From the standards development page, describing why the council writes its own reliability standards.

claims.claim: The interconnected Railbelt bulk electric system serves a geographic area entirely inside Alaska.
claims.value: Fairbanks and Delta Junction to Homer and Seldovia
claims.verbatim: The interconnected Railbelt BES serves the geographic area of Alaska extending from the communities of Fairbanks and Delta Junction in the north; south to Homer and Seldovia
claims.notes: Continues west to Tyonek and east to Glacier View, Seward and Whittier. Every named boundary is an Alaska community.

claims.claim: Five load-serving electric utilities are interconnected on the Alaska Railbelt.
claims.verbatim: five load-serving electric utilities interconnected across nearly 700 miles of Alaska's rugged landscape.
claims.notes: Golden Valley Electric Association, Matanuska Electric Association, Chugach Electric Association, Homer Electric Association and Seward Electric System.

claims.claim: The Railbelt Reliability Council says the Railbelt grid serves nearly three-quarters of Alaska's population.
claims.verbatim: our responsibility is to ensure a reliable, efficient, and sustainable electric grid for nearly three-quarters of Alaska's population.
claims.notes: The council's own characterisation. Attribute it rather than stating it flat.

claims.claim: The Railbelt utilities are interconnected across nearly 700 miles.
claims.verbatim: interconnected across nearly 700 miles of Alaska's rugged landscape.

claims.claim: The Alaska Intertie is owned by the Alaska Energy Authority and runs 170 miles between Willow and Healy.
claims.verbatim: transmission line between Willow and Healy
claims.notes: Page also gives 170-mile long and owned by the Alaska Energy Authority.

claims.claim: The Alaska Intertie was built to 345 kilovolt standards and operates at 138 kilovolts, per the Alaska Energy Authority.
claims.verbatim: 345 kilovolt (kV) transmission line between Willow and Healy
claims.notes: The page carries both the 345 kV construction figure and the phrase operates at 138 kV. Either number sits far above the order's 69,000 volt line.

claims.claim: The Alaska Energy Authority calls the Alaska Intertie an integral part of the interconnected bulk electrical system for the Railbelt region.
claims.verbatim: As an integral part of the interconnected Bulk Electrical System (BES) for the railbelt region, this AEA owned asset transmits Bradley Lake and economy power north into the GVEA system.
claims.notes: A state agency using the exact term of art the executive order builds its scope on. Cuts toward the order reaching Alaska, and is the deck's counterweight.

claims.claim: Chugach Electric Association serves nearly 89,000 members at over 113,000 metered locations.
claims.verbatim: serving nearly 89,000 members at over 113,000 metered locations
claims.notes: Largest of the five Railbelt utilities.

claims.claim: Homer Electric Association reports 26,181 member-owners.
claims.verbatim: 26,181 Member-Owners
claims.notes: Utility's own about page, current as published.

claims.claim: Alaska generated 6,690,506 megawatthours of electricity in 2024.
claims.notes: EIA Alaska Electricity Profile 2024. Total retail sales on the same page are 6,046,503 megawatthours.

claims.claim: Alaska's average retail electricity price across all sectors in 2024 was 22.17 cents per kilowatthour.
claims.notes: EIA Alaska Electricity Profile 2024. Do not blend with the repo's monthly power.json series, which is a different cadence.

claims.claim: FERC accepted for filing a preliminary permit application from DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, LLC under Project No. 15423-000.
claims.verbatim: [Project No. 15423-000]
claims.source_outlet: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission via Federal Register
claims.notes: Notice dated September 1st, 2026, published September 4th at page 56879. The bracketed docket line prints without a P- prefix.

claims.claim: The DeepGreen Cook Inlet project proposes an approximately 3.5 mile 115 kilovolt hybrid power and fiber-optic armored subsea cable.
claims.verbatim: an approximately 3.5-mile long, 115 kV hybrid power/fiber-optic armored subsea cable
claims.source_outlet: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission via Federal Register
claims.notes: 115 kV is above the executive order's 69,000 volt line.

claims.claim: The DeepGreen Cook Inlet project proposes 66 modular subsea-compute hives described as data center pods.
claims.verbatim: 66 modular subsea-compute hives (data center pods)
claims.source_outlet: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission via Federal Register
claims.notes: A preliminary permit is a study permit and not construction authorisation. Say proposes.

claims.claim: The DeepGreen Cook Inlet project proposes approximately 330 to 350 marine hydrokinetic turbines.
claims.verbatim: approximately 330-350 marine hydrokinetic turbines
claims.source_outlet: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission via Federal Register
claims.notes: Upper Cook Inlet, East Foreland Corridor, Kenai Peninsula Borough.

claims.claim: The FERC notice puts the DeepGreen project's estimated annual generation at 100 megawatts.
claims.verbatim: The estimated annual generation of the DeepGreen Project would be 100 megawatts
claims.source_outlet: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission via Federal Register
claims.notes: UNIT PROBLEM IN THE SOURCE. Annual generation is energy and belongs in megawatthours, and the notice states megawatts. Quote the notice and attribute it. Never silently convert.

claims.claim: Comments and competing applications on the DeepGreen preliminary permit are due by 5 p.m. Eastern on November 2nd, 2026.
claims.verbatim: by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on November 2, 2026
claims.source_outlet: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission via Federal Register
claims.notes: Sixty days from the notice date of September 1st, 2026.

killed.claim: The DOE request for information carries docket number DOE-HQ-2026-1123.
killed.why: The document prints two different strings. The bracketed header line reads DOE-2026-HQ-2026-1123 and the regulations.gov path matches it, while the ADDRESSES prose refers to DOE-HQ-2026-1123. Two fetches reproduced the doubled form. Cite RIN 1901-AB79 instead, which is unambiguous.

killed.claim: The DeepGreen FERC docket is P-15423-000.
killed.why: The notice prints the bracketed docket line as Project No. 15423-000 with no P- prefix.

killed.claim: The words interconnection and interconnected appear nowhere in Executive Order 14421.
killed.why: FALSE. Interconnected appears in Section 5(a)(i). That phrase is the load-bearing element of the whole story, so the absence claim is limited to Alaska, Hawaii, islanded and non-contiguous.

killed.claim: The word interconnection appears nowhere in the DOE request for information.
killed.why: Only one fetch supported it and the distinction between interconnection and interconnected is too fine to publish on a single read.

killed.claim: The DOE request for information is the document that will set the covered scope of the order.
killed.why: Editorial characterisation, not what the document says. The RFI seeks information to inform DOE actions to implement the order. The 120 day rulemaking sets scope. Replaced by C18.

killed.claim: Alaska is outside the NERC-registered bulk electric system and outside every NERC interconnection.
killed.why: Could not be established. nerc.com returned 403 on two pages, and the EIA interconnections material speaks only of the Lower 48 without naming Alaska. The statutory exclusion at 16 U.S.C. 824o(k) is verified and is the cleaner fact.

killed.claim: The Alaska Railbelt is not electrically connected to any grid outside Alaska.
killed.why: No source states this in those words. Publish C24 and C25, attributed, rather than a bare negative the sourcing does not carry.

killed.claim: The Railbelt's peak load is a stated number of megawatts.
killed.why: No figure found on any reachable primary page. Leave peak load out of the deck entirely.

killed.claim: NREL found the Railbelt can reach about 76 percent renewable generation by 2040 at lowest cost.
killed.why: The full-text PDF would not parse, and it is a projection and off-story.

killed.claim: An identified Alaska utility purchases specific covered equipment categories.
killed.why: Could not be sourced. The Regulatory Commission of Alaska returns 403, no utility board packet was reachable in HTML, and no EIA surface carries equipment procurement. Nothing on this point appears in the deck.

killed.claim: EIA states that Alaska has its own separate grid not connected to the contiguous United States.
killed.why: Not found. The EIA explainer covers the Lower 48 only and does not mention Alaska or Hawaii.

killed.claim: Chugach Electric operates transmission at specified voltages over a specified number of line miles.
killed.why: The Chugach about page gives members and service area only, and its company-facts URL 404s. GVEA returned 403 on two URLs.

killed.claim: The Southern Intertie between the Kenai Peninsula and Anchorage is a 138 kilovolt line.
killed.why: Only supportable from a 2002 USDA Rural Utilities Service notice, twenty-four years outside the window and describing a proposal. Dropped rather than published with a caveat, because C30's Alaska Intertie figure already carries the point from a current source.
